name: Graph Subset Problem
description: You are given an undirected graph with $$$n$$$ vertices and $$$m$$$ edges. Also, you are given an integer $$$k$$$. Find either a clique of size $$$k$$$ or a non-empty subset of vertices such that each vertex of this subset has at least $$$k$$$ neighbors in the subset. If there are no such cliques and subsets report about it. A subset of vertices is called a clique of size $$$k$$$ if its size is $$$k$$$ and there exists an edge between every two vertices from the subset. A vertex is called a neighbor of the other vertex if there exists an edge between them.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^5$$$) — the number of test cases. The next lines contain descriptions of test cases. The first line of the description of each test case contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq n, m, k \leq 10^5$$$, $$$k \leq n$$$). Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u, v$$$ $$$(1 \leq u, v \leq n, u \neq v)$$$, denoting an edge between vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$. It is guaranteed that there are no self-loops or multiple edges. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ for all test cases and the sum of $$$m$$$ for all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case: If you found a subset of vertices such that each vertex of this subset has at least $$$k$$$ neighbors in the subset in the first line output $$$1$$$ and the size of the subset. On the second line output the vertices of the subset in any order. If you found a clique of size $$$k$$$ then in the first line output $$$2$$$ and in the second line output the vertices of the clique in any order. If there are no required subsets and cliques print $$$-1$$$. If there exists multiple possible answers you can print any of them.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1439B — Graph Subset Problem [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
